article.overview: A soil cohesion tester is a payload concept for measuring how strongly lunar regolith holds together, a property that affects whether the ground can carry a rover wheel or lander footpad, how a trench or borehole keeps its shape, and how excavation hardware will perform. No flown, prototype or proposed lunar instrument carrying this exact name was identified in this review. The nearest real instruments are soil-mechanics experiments from the Surveyor, Apollo and Lunokhod programmes and a proposed Chang'e 8 instrument. They infer cohesion and friction indirectly from penetration, shear or trenching tests [1][2][3][5]. This entry therefore describes the measurement class and its heritage rather than a verified single design.
article.description: Cohesion is the part of a soil's shear strength that does not depend on the load pressing the soil together. Soil engineers normally report it alongside the internal friction angle, because the two define the Mohr-Coulomb failure relation used to predict when ground will fail [1][2]. Three measurement approaches are used. A cone is pushed into the ground and the resistance is recorded against depth (penetrometry). A bladed vane is rotated in the soil and the torque needed to shear the soil is recorded (vane shear). A confined sample or a box is sheared under a known normal load (direct shear). Each approach has been used in lunar or lunar-analogue work. The Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer used penetration [1]. The Surveyor soil mechanics surface sampler used a motor-driven scoop, and its motor current was measured during the tests [3][4]. The Soviet Lunokhod rovers carried a cone penetrometer and a shear vane [9]. A Caltech technical report describes a box-in-box device for in situ direct shear and sinkage tests [6], and a proposed Chang'e 8 instrument combines a cone penetrometer and a shear vane in one vane-cone with a permittivity sensor [5]. Cohesion is difficult to measure on the Moon because regolith is a dry granular material whose strength changes with density, depth and disturbance. Test results on lunar simulants also depend on the method. One University of Vermont study reports that vertical-cut cohesion estimates rose steadily with relative density for the JSC-1A and GRC-3 simulants, whereas simple direct-shear estimates showed no clear trend [8]. That finding comes from a search excerpt, because the page could not be read in full. A related but different NASA investigation, Regolith Adherence Characterization (RAC), was planned for Blue Ghost Mission 1 to expose 15 sample materials to the lunar environment and measure how strongly regolith sticks to them [7]. RAC measures adhesion to surfaces, not the internal cohesion of soil, so it is not a cohesion tester. Its flight outcome was not verified in this review.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: A soil cohesion tester would support both engineering and science. For engineering, cohesion and friction control rover trafficability, the bearing capacity under a landing pad, the stability of excavated walls, and the force needed to drill or dig. For science, a density or strength profile with depth can help interpret how the regolith was formed and how impacts have mixed it. The proposed Chang'e 8 instrument would also estimate bulk density and ice content from permittivity measurements [5]. The Caltech report describes its device as a compact but accurate tool for regolith testing on rovers or other exploratory vehicles [6]. These are proposed applications. No flown result from a dedicated cohesion tester was identified.
article.operating_principle: No single operating principle applies, because each method measures a different response. In penetrometry, the force needed to push a cone is recorded against depth. The Apollo 16 Self-Recording Penetrometer page states that cohesion and friction can be solved from penetration resistance when two cone sizes or two depths are available in a homogeneous soil [1]. In vane shear, the torque against rotation angle gives the shear resistance, and the proposed TTI measures shear strength as a function of shear angle [5]. In direct shear, a normal load is applied to a confined soil and the shear force is recorded as the box moves. The Caltech device is designed to yield Coulomb parameters, including cohesion and internal friction angle, together with Bekker parameters [6]. Every method depends on assumptions about density and homogeneity, and those assumptions control the reduced cohesion value [1][2].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar regolith strength is poorly measured in situ. The proposed TTI abstract states that regolith strength data are scarce because modern landing missions have not carried dedicated instruments for it [5]. The Apollo and Lunokhod measurements remain the main in-situ benchmarks for surface soil strength [1][9], but they are limited in number and location, and their interpretation depends on assumed density and laboratory data [2]. A modern instrument that measures cohesion, friction and density at a known location would add a data set that is largely missing from the lunar surface record.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a soil cohesion tester. The examples below cover one historical Apollo penetrometer, one Surveyor soil-mechanics scoop, Soviet Lunokhod cone and vane devices, one proposed Chang'e 8 instrument and one Caltech engineering device. Values are given only where a cited source states them; otherwise they are recorded as null. The examples are not directly comparable, because they measure different responses over different depths.

examples.name: Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer (SRP)
examples.type: Historical lunar penetrometer for soil-mechanics measurements
examples.flight_status: Flown on Apollo 16, as described in the source read. An Apollo 15 SRP is mentioned in search excerpts but was not verified in full text.
examples.recording: Penetration depth referenced to a surface reference plane; results inscribed on a recording drum in the upper housing. Force transducer not described in the text read.
examples.cohesion_and_friction: No numerical cohesion or friction angle in the source read. The ratio delta/phi is stated as 0.5 (dimensionless), from friction tests between a ground basalt simulant and hard anodised aluminium. Search-excerpt summaries (Apollo 16: cohesion about 0.1 to 1.0 kN/m2, friction angle 30 to 50 degrees; Apollo 15: friction angle 35 to 40 degrees, small cohesion) were not verified against full text and are not used as specifications.

examples.name: Surveyor Soil Mechanics Surface Sampler (SMSS)
examples.type: Historical lunar soil-mechanics scoop mounted on a spacecraft arm
examples.flight_status: Flown on Surveyor 3. Moved from later Surveyor missions and adapted to the mounting location and electronics interface of the approach television camera.
examples.modifications: Strain, acceleration and position sensors removed; motor current measurement added.
examples.operation: Search excerpts describe the scoop digging trenches imaged by the television camera; not verified in full text.
examples.cohesion: A search excerpt of the Apollo 12 soil mechanics analysis describes the soil as weakly cohesive, medium-dense granular material, consistent with Surveyor results. Not verified.

examples.name: Lunokhod cone penetrometer and shear vane
examples.flight_status: Carried on the Lunokhod rovers. A secondary review excerpt refers to a combined cone-and-vane tester called PROP; not verified in a primary source.
examples.measurements: Cone penetration resistance and vane shear strength.
examples.dimensions: A 1972 NASA report appears to list cone and vane dimensions; only a garbled OCR excerpt was read, so no values are recorded. The original scan should be checked.

examples.name: Chang'e 8 Terrain Testing Instrument (TTI), proposed
examples.flight_status: Planned for the Chang'e 8 landing and roving mission in 2029. Structural model delivered; electrical model planned for summer 2026. Not flown.
examples.measurements: Penetration resistance from a cone penetrometer driven by a linear translation mechanism; shear strength from a rotating front shear vane; bulk density and ice content inferred from a permittivity sensor whose electrodes are integrated with the shear vanes.
examples.mass_note: Approximately 1.5 kg including an electronics unit housed inside the rover.
examples.operations: Multiple measurements at different sites during the first lunar day, using the JINNAH-1 rover provided by SUPARCO.

examples.name: Caltech in situ direct shear and sinkage device
examples.type: Engineering device described in a 2013 technical report; no flight status
examples.design: A box nested within a larger box, both open at the bottom. Two rotating plates on the outer box swing outward so the inner box can shear without surrounding soil resisting it.
examples.outputs: Coulomb parameters including cohesion and internal friction angle, and Bekker parameters.
examples.measured_values: Not reported in the abstract read; full report not reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a soil cohesion tester. The Apollo SRP's 76 cm penetration range, the Caltech device's nested-box geometry and the proposed TTI's depth range of about 5 cm describe different instruments and cannot be combined into a class value.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The only mass in this entry is the proposed TTI's approximately 1.5 kg, which includes an electronics unit housed inside the rover. It comes from a proposed design. Apollo SRP, SMSS, Lunokhod and Caltech mass values were not verified and are recorded as null.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No verified power figures were identified for any example; all are recorded as null.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The instrument would operate in vacuum, with extreme surface temperature swings and exposure to abrasive, adhesive dust. Its reaction forces must be carried by the lander or rover, so the reference surface and arm stiffness matter. The Apollo SRP used a surface reference plane to define depth, and a rover-mounted tester depends on the reach and stiffness of its arm. Penetration and shear depths are limited by design: the Apollo SRP reached 76 cm, and the proposed TTI measures to about 5 cm. Near-surface measurements are influenced by disturbance from landing and mobility activity, so placement and timing of measurements need control. These are engineering considerations rather than verified requirements for a named mission.
article.limitations: - Cohesion and friction are inferred rather than measured directly, and the inference depends on assumed density, homogeneity and the chosen model. - Depth is limited: about 5 cm for the proposed TTI and 76 cm for the Apollo SRP. Surface disturbance and layering can dominate shallow results. - Simulant results depend on the test method and density. - No dedicated lunar cohesion measurement has been verified as flown; the flight record is limited to related penetrometer, scoop and cone-and-vane experiments.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A soil cohesion tester would be integrated on a lander or rover and delivered as part of that spacecraft's payload, with Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer and landing loads following the usual surface-payload chain. The proposed TTI is designed to operate from the JINNAH-1 rover, and its electronics unit is accommodated inside that rover. The Surveyor SMSS was mounted on the spacecraft arm and adapted to the approach television camera's mounting location and electronics interface. The Apollo SRP was an astronaut-operated instrument, as described in search excerpts and not verified in full text.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument on a lander or rover on Earth.
Launch the spacecraft and transfer it to the Moon.
Land the payload and deliver it to the surface on the lander or rover.
Stow, release or deploy the instrument, which may be handheld by astronauts, arm-mounted, or rover-mounted depending on design.
Connect power and data, and establish a stable reference for depth and orientation before measurement.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: A handheld tool needs astronaut time and a stable reference. A robotic arm needs reach and stiffness. A rover-mounted tester needs stowage, release and traverse operation. The Apollo SRP was astronaut-operated; the Surveyor SMSS was arm-mounted; the proposed TTI is rover-mounted.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo SRP (astronaut-operated penetrometer, Apollo 16), Surveyor 3 SMSS (arm-mounted scoop), Lunokhod cone penetrometer and shear vane (rover-mounted).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander or rover is asserted here, because verified interface data (mass, dimensions, mounting, power and data interfaces) were not reviewed for any named spacecraft.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo penetrometers and the Surveyor soil-mechanics scoop were among the first instruments to infer lunar surface strength from mechanical tests on the Moon [1][3]. The Surveyor 3 SMSS paper is a primary record of an in-situ soil-mechanics device on a lunar lander [3]. The Lunokhod cone and vane devices added a second, independent set of surface measurements [9]. These heritage experiments shaped the strength values still used as benchmarks, although later analyses note that the Apollo-era interpretations relied on assumptions [2]. The proposed Chang'e 8 TTI would revisit this measurement class with newer instrumentation, but its results are not yet available [5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name 'soil cohesion tester' describes a payload class rather than an identified flown or proposed instrument, so no single set of specifications can be verified. The Apollo 16 soil mechanics report [2] is a scanned PDF that could not be read in this review, and the cohesion and friction ranges quoted from search excerpts for the Apollo 15 and 16 penetrometers remain unverified. The Apollo 15 soil mechanics chapter returned a 404 error and was not read. The UVM simulant summary [8], the Lunokhod report [9], the RAC-1 flight status [7] and an arXiv review of rheological simulants were available only as search excerpts or in unreadable form, so they are treated as leads rather than verified facts. The SMSS and Lunokhod dimensional and mass values were not verified. A stock-photo caption gives 111 N as the maximum Apollo SRP force, which conflicts with the 215 N stated on the Apollo 16 SRP page [1]; the primary page value is used. No image asset was verified, so no image is included in this article.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue entry 165 'Soil cohesion tester' (category 8, Regolith and soil analysis) names a payload class; no flown, prototype or proposed instrument with this exact name was identified.

Apollo 16 SRP values (maximum depth 76 cm; maximum recordable force 215 N; plate and cone dimensions) are taken from the Apollo 16 SRP page read in full. A stock-photo caption gives 111 N; this conflicts and was not used.

Apollo 15 and 16 cohesion and friction ranges come from search excerpts. The Apollo 16 soil mechanics report is a scanned PDF that could not be read, and the Apollo 15 soil mechanics chapter returned a 404 error. These values are unverified and not used as specifications.
Surveyor SMSS trenching and Apollo 12 cohesion description come from search excerpts and an abstract-level Caltech record; the full 1968 and 1969 papers were not read.
Lunokhod dimensional values were only visible in a garbled OCR excerpt and are deliberately not recorded.
The UVM simulant study, the RAC-1 flight status and the Lunokhod report were available only as search excerpts or in unreadable form; the RAC-1 outcome was not verified.
Chang'e 8 TTI values (depth about 5 cm, mass about 1.5 kg) are from a conference abstract for a planned mission and are not flight data.
No image asset was verified. Image arrays are empty, and research_status image flags are false.
